detailed_analysis: The pattern is fit as 32 split pseudo-Voigt reflections on a SNIP background over 5-45 deg, achieving global R^2 = 0.9999996 and peak_region_R^2 = 0.9997. The strong, isolated reflections at 11.93 deg (amplitude ~1.27e6, area ~3.47e5) and 19.99 deg (amplitude ~1.02e6, area ~2.93e5) dominate the pattern, with secondary strong features at 15.95 and 17.89 deg. FWHMs of the well-defined mid-angle reflections cluster around 0.25-0.31 deg, corresponding to microcrystalline domains of ~25-32 nm by Scherrer. This is internally consistent for the bulk of the peaks and represents the robust size result. However, the full per-peak Scherrer set spans 7 to 140 nm (>3x, in fact ~20x), which by the domain rules indicates anisotropic broadening and/or unreliable widths for a few peaks: the two ~140 nm and ~139 nm values come from very narrow (~0.057 deg) low-index peaks near 5 deg that sit on the residual tail of the excluded air-scatter climb and are likely contaminated/instrument-limited, while the ~7 nm value (peak_13, FWHM 1.1 deg) is a broad, low-amplitude feature likely absorbing background curvature or overlap rather than a real nanocrystalline domain. The Williamson-Hall analysis is diagnostic: R^2 = 0.012 (essentially zero correlation), so the size-strain decomposition (nominal 30 nm, strain 0.0011) must NOT be reported as physical - the linear W-H model does not apply, consistent with anisotropic/mixed broadening. Several eta values pinned at exactly 0 (pure Lorentzian) or 1 (pure Gaussian) show the mixing is unconstrained for those peaks. The apex residuals at 11.9 and 20 deg are the expected profile limit for the sharpest cores and, given this is an in-situ dehydration ramp, may also carry a small physical signature of evolving strain/lattice contraction; they do not indicate a missing reflection. Because this is a single frame of a variable-temperature series, position shifts across frames (lattice change) are expected and are the point of the experiment. The most defensible quantitative outcome is a microcrystalline domain size of ~30 nm (2 sig figs) from the well-behaved mid-angle reflections, reported as a range (~25-32 nm) and explicitly flagged as anisotropic, with the outlier peaks excluded.

scientific_claims.claim: The dominant crystalline phase has a coherent domain size of ~30 nm (range ~25-32 nm across well-defined mid-angle reflections; +/-15% typical accuracy), i.e. microcrystalline, with broadening that is anisotropic rather than uniform (Williamson-Hall R^2 = 0.012 rules out an isotropic size+strain decomposition).
scientific_claims.scientific_impact: Tracking coherent domain size and its anisotropy through an in-situ dehydration ramp constrains how the framework crystallites reorganize (dehydration-induced contraction, defect formation, or directional coarsening) and distinguishes size effects from microstrain during the transformation.
scientific_claims.has_anyone_question: Has anyone observed anisotropic ~30 nm coherent domain sizes and non-linear Williamson-Hall behavior in a framework/hydrate material during in-situ synchrotron dehydration, and how does the domain size evolve across the dehydration ramp?

model_type: Sum of split (asymmetric) pseudo-Voigt peaks on SNIP background (snip_iterations=auto), single global fit_pattern; auto peak detection (prominence_frac=0.005, min_distance_deg=0.05) with explicit seed centers 11.6/17.65/20.9 bootstrapping the three verifier-flagged under-modelled features into the single global fit; eta free per peak, FWHM in [0.05,2.0]; fit_range=(5.0,45.0) to exclude the low-angle air-scatter/beamstop climb

verification_iterations.model: Sum of split (asymmetric) pseudo-Voigt profiles, one per Bragg reflection, on a SNIP background. eta (Gaussian-Lorentzian mixing) free per peak in [0,1]. Expected ~7–10 significant reflections: ~12.0°, ~17.5° (shoulder), ~17.85°, ~20.0° (strong isolated), ~28.2° (broad), ~29.6°, ~29.85° (shoulder), plus weaker high-angle features. Peaks within 1.5×FWHM (the 17.5/17.85 pair and the 29.6/29.85 pair) fit jointly within the single global model. Split pseudo-Voigt captures sharp-peak asymmetry natively.

issues.problem: Under-resolved structure: the data shows a clear shoulder/second maximum near x≈17.6-17.7 rising into a taller peak at x≈17.9 that a single asymmetric peak (peak_5) cannot describe.
Unmodelled shoulder/intensity on the high-angle side of the main 20.0 reflection produces a coherent residual bump.
Residual oscillation on the strong 11.9 reflection indicates a small unresolved feature/asymmetry on the low-angle flank.

verification_iterations.fix_applied: Add peak components seeded at x≈17.65, x≈20.9, and x≈11.6 (e.g. lower prominence_frac toward 0.005 or pass explicit peak_centers including these positions) and refit within the current split-pseudo-Voigt model.

verification_iterations.model: Sum of split (asymmetric) pseudo-Voigt profiles, one per Bragg reflection, on a SNIP background. eta (Gaussian-Lorentzian mixing) free per peak in [0,1]. Now expecting ~10-13 significant reflections after resolving three additional under-modelled features flagged by verification: ~12.0° (with a resolved low-angle flank feature near ~11.6°), ~17.5° (shoulder), ~17.65° (newly resolved second maximum distinct from the 17.9 peak), ~17.85/17.9°, ~20.0° (strong isolated), ~20.9° (newly resolved shoulder on high-angle side, between the 20.0 and 21.5 reflections), ~21.5°, ~28.2° (broad), ~29.6°, ~29.85° (shoulder), plus weaker high-angle features. Closely spaced peaks (the 11.6/11.9 pair, the 17.5/17.65/17.9 cluster, the 20.0/20.9 pair, and the 29.6/29.85 pair) fit jointly within the single global model. Split pseudo-Voigt captures native sharp-peak asymmetry; the added components resolve residual structure that exceeds what single-peak asymmetry can describe.
